summary: Examines a synchronization problem in SMTP that can cause a message to be delivered more than once, and suggests a way to avoid it. Some familiarity with the SMTP specification in RFC 821 is required.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1047 explains how an SMTP connection failure can make both mail systems keep a copy of the same message. The receiver should acknowledge promptly after safely queuing the message, and the sender should allow enough time for that reply.

questions: why do duplicate emails happen with smtp
how to avoid duplicate message delivery in smtp
how to prevent duplicate mail delivery
subtitle: Why SMTP can deliver a message twice when the final acknowledgment is lost.

tldr.problem: At the end of SMTP delivery, the receiver may accept a message while the sender still lacks confirmation that delivery succeeded.
tldr.mechanism: If the connection fails before the sender receives the final 250 reply, the sender retries even though the receiver may already have the message.
tldr.outcome: The RFC recommends acknowledging once the message is safely queued and suggests a longer timeout for the final reply.

facts.label: Suggested reply timeout
facts.value: At least 5 minutes; 10 minutes is reasonable

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 1047's status as Unknown. The memo examines a synchronization problem in SMTP and suggests ways mailers can reduce duplicate delivery.

sections.title: The Gap Between Acceptance and Confirmation
sections.content:
After sending the message text, the sender transmits a line containing a single dot. The receiving mailer then processes the message and either accepts it with a 250 reply or rejects it.

There is a period after the receiver decides to accept the message but before the sender receives the reply. During this synchronization gap, the receiver treats the message as delivered while the sender must still assume it was not delivered. If the connection fails then, both sides may try to deliver their copies.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver can accept a message before the sender hears that it succeeded. If the connection breaks in between, the sender may send the message again.

sections.title: Why the Gap Can Last
sections.content:
Some mailers delay the final reply while they perform additional processing. The RFC gives examples such as expanding a mailing list or trying to place the message into local mailboxes before confirming acceptance.

Those steps can keep both copies active for minutes, increasing the chance of a timeout or network failure before the sender receives the 250 reply.
sections.plainLanguage: Extra work before the receiver replies makes the uncertain period longer. A timeout or broken connection during that period can cause another delivery attempt.

sections.title: Acknowledge After Safe Queuing
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that receiving mailers shorten the gap by acknowledging the final dot as soon as possible and doing more complex processing later. It says a receiver can reply after placing the message safely in a non-volatile queue, such as on disk.

The memo also recommends configuring mailers to do less processing before the reply. It says the timeout for the final response should probably be at least 5 minutes and that 10 minutes would not be unreasonable.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver can confirm the message once it is safely stored, then do additional work later. A longer sender timeout also gives the receiver more time to reply.
